newsitem.title: UK: Swiss accounts hold memories, money for Britons.
newsitem.headline: Swiss accounts hold memories, money for Britons.

text.p: Barring an amazing coincidence, Fiona Goetz believes she has found her late husband's name on a list of 40 Britons who have held Swiss bank accounts since World War Two.
"I had heard that there was a Walter Goetz on the list, but I did not think it could possibly be my husband, as there was never any mention of the account in the family," she said.

Her interest was piqued when Swiss banks broke decades of silence by revealing in newspapers around the world the names listed on dormant Swiss bank accounts that were opened in the World War Two era. The accounts are presumed to include many opened by Jews who were trying to hide their assets from the Nazis and were killed in the Holocaust.

Goetz is a common name in Germany, but what convinced Fiona that the account was her husband's were the names of those having power of attorney over the account. They fitted the names of his parents, one of whom, Jeanne, was French-born.
"Of course I cannot say for sure, but it would seem a very far-fetched coincidence," she told Reuters by telephone.
Her husband died two years ago. His father died during the 1930s and his mother in the 1970s. The existence of a Swiss bank account was never mentioned in the family, Fiona Goetz said.
She now plans to contact accountants Ernst and Young for further information about the claims process. "There is no point the Swiss giving this information if relatives don't follow it up," she said.
"I think anybody who had been there during that very difficult turmoil...there would always be something those who came after them would not know," she said.
British families of Holocaust victims crowded into a central London cafe on Wednesday to check on the Internet computer network if their relatives were on the list of account-holders.

A telephone hotline set up by the Holocaust Educational Trust received about 80 calls during the day. Two people had recognised the names of their grandparents among names also printed on three pages in the Times newspaper.
But no one had come forward with a definite claim on the dormant accounts, a spokeswoman for the trust said.
"It's all a bit of a shock for them. Most of the calls have been from people wondering what the next step is if the names they are looking for are not on the list," she said.
Some people had rung the hotline to say they recognised names and pass on information about the families concerned.
The trust said it wanted more information to be released to help those trying to trace funds deposited by Holocaust victims.

"There are all sorts of details they could give, such as addresses, ages of account holders and the dates the accounts were opened," said Greville Janner, member of parliament and the trust's chairman.
"No bank will take money on the basis of just a name, especially not the Swiss, who are very meticulous."
